core: Working definition of hydration: maintaining the body's water balance, with fluid intake roughly matching fluid loss (attributed to MedlinePlus and OpenStax framing)
Why the balance matters, each named with one line: blood volume and transport, temperature regulation through perspiration, digestion, and concentration/cognitive sharpness
Thirst as the body's main signal and the honest note that it is a late one (fires after fluid is already depleted; even mild dehydration can produce symptoms)

How much: the general adult guidance (IOM DRI 2.7-3.7 L total incl. food; Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics ~11.5/15.5 cups; NAM ~13/9 cups fluids) stated as general guidance, not a prescription, with 'no specific recommendation' acknowledged
Sources: plain water, other beverages (milk, tea, coffee, juice, soup), and water-rich foods (~20% of intake); alcohol does not add water
Overhydration is rare in healthy people (honest note, stated simply)
Honest framing: hydration is a daily habit, not a competition; urine color as the rough gauge
supporting: Water makes up more than two-thirds of body weight and ~60% of adult body weight
Water has zero calories; plain water is the best choice for most people
Fluid needs rise with heat, exercise, fever, and fluid losses
Older adults often lose part of their sense of thirst
Mild dehydration symptoms can appear at as little as a 2% water deficit

claims.claim: Hydration is maintaining the body's water balance: keeping fluid intake roughly matched to fluid loss, so body fluids stay balanced and every cell, tissue, and organ has the water it needs.
Water is the basis for the body's fluids and makes up more than two-thirds of the weight of the human body (about 60% of adult body weight).
Water matters for blood volume and transport: molecules dissolve into the watery blood environment and move through the body, and blood carries breakdown products away for elimination.
Water regulates body temperature through perspiration (sweating), the body's built-in cooling mechanism.
Water supports digestion: it makes up saliva, helps move food through the intestines, helps prevent constipation, and is necessary for proper digestion.
Even mild dehydration — as little as a 2% water deficit — can produce fatigue, confusion or short-term memory trouble, and mood changes such as irritability.

Thirst is the body's major signal that fluid is running low, but it is a late one: it fires when the body is already somewhat depleted, and even mild dehydration can already be producing symptoms; older adults in particular lose part of their sense of thirst as they age.

There is no specific recommendation for how much water each person should drink; the adult guidance is general: IOM Dietary Reference Intake 91-125 fl oz (2.7-3.7 L) per day total including food; Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics about 11.5 cups (women) and 15.5 cups (men) total including food, roughly 20% of which comes from food (about 9 and 13 cups from beverages); National Academy of Medicine adequate intake about 13 cups (men) and 9 cups (women) of fluids, described as a general guide, not a daily target.

Daily fluid intake comes from plain water (the best choice for most people; zero calories), other beverages (milk, tea, coffee, juice, soup, drinking water), and water-rich foods such as fruits and vegetables, which supply about 20% of total intake; alcohol does not add to the body's water because it acts as a diuretic.

Overhydration is rare in healthy people: the body usually excretes extra water through urine and sweat (no upper intake level has been set for water); water toxicity and hyponatremia are possible only in rare circumstances, such as drinking a very large volume in a short time, or with kidney problems, extreme heat stress, or prolonged strenuous exercise.
Urine color is a rough everyday gauge of hydration status: darker urine indicates a greater need for fluid, and pale yellow indicates the balance is roughly fine.

conflictingEvidence.issue: The daily water guidance numbers differ across authoritative sources (IOM DRI 2.7-3.7 L total; Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics 11.5/15.5 cups total; NAM adequate intake 13/9 cups of fluids).
positions: MedlinePlus (IOM DRI): 91-125 fl oz (2.7-3.7 L) per day for adults, total from food and beverages.
OpenStax (Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics): about 11.5 cups/day women and 15.5 cups/day men, including food; about 20% from food, so about 9 and 13 cups from beverages.
Harvard (National Academy of Medicine): about 13 cups men and 9 cups women of daily fluids, 'not a daily target, but a general guide.'
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The figures are consistent once the frame is clear: roughly 2.7-3.7 L (11-16 cups) of total water per day including food, with about 9-13 cups coming from beverages. The lesson presents the cluster as general guidance with attribution, explicitly notes that no specific per-person recommendation exists, and avoids presenting any single number as a prescription.

conflictingEvidence.issue: The popular 'eight glasses a day' rule versus current guidance.
positions: Popular advice: everyone should aim for eight 8-ounce glasses of water daily.

Harvard Nutrition Source: the rule 'may not be appropriate for every person'; NAM amounts 'are not a daily target, but a general guide.' MedlinePlus: 'There is no specific recommendation for how much water you should drink.'
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson treats 'eight glasses' as a memory aid, not a requirement, and leads with the sourced general guidance plus the honest note that needs vary by person and day.

sourceRecords.title: Dehydration (Health Topics)
sourceRecords.notes: Read 2026-08-22 via direct fetch. Supports: dehydration defined as losing more fluids than the body takes in so it lacks enough fluids to work properly; body fluids out of balance; causes (diarrhea, vomiting, sweating too much, fever, not drinking enough); older adults may lose their sense of thirst as they age; symptoms include dark-colored urine, tiredness, dizziness; severe dehydration can be life-threatening. Facts synthesized only.
